title: Optimal Protocols for Studying & Learning: Self-Testing, Focus, Sleep and Spacing
summary: Huberman argues learning is about offsetting forgetting, and that self-testing soon after first exposure beats rereading by a wide margin. He covers the two-step plasticity process (focus, then sleep), habits of top students, NSDR, gap effects, emotion and interleaving.

principles.text: Treat studying as offsetting forgetting, not just absorbing information.
principles.quote: Rather than think about studying to learn and retain information. I want you to think about studying to offset the natural process of forgetting

principles.text: Test yourself rather than rereading; testing is the best studying tool, not just evaluation.
principles.quote: reading and rereading material and re-re-re-rereading material is far less effective than reading material and then thinking about that material, testing yourself on that material

principles.text: Self-test soon after first exposure, ideally the same or next day, then again after a long delay.
principles.quote: Test yourself on the material that you were just exposed to very soon after your first exposure to it because that offsets the natural forgetting of new material

principles.text: Prefer open-ended, short-answer self-tests over multiple choice, which only trains familiarity.
principles.quote: The best tests are open-ended, short answer, very minimal prompt tests

principles.text: Learning is two steps: alert, focused attention first, then neuroplastic change during deep sleep, so sleep well the first night.
principles.quote: Neuroplasticity and learning, that is converting your studying efforts into retention of knowledge, is a two-step process.

principles.text: Train focus with 5 to 10 minutes of daily mindfulness or a visual focusing exercise, and expect strain to feel productive.
principles.quote: the strain that you feel in forcing yourself to learn how to focus, that is good
